steps.title: Import React and useState from 'react'
steps.instruction: Import React and the useState hook from the 'react' package. This is the foundation for building React components with state.
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in React and useState from 'react'. The syntax is: import React, { useState } from 'react';
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of importing React and useState
import React, { useState } from 'react';
steps.seedCode: // Import React and useState from 'react' here
steps.expectedOutcome: The import statement for React and useState is added, making them available for use in the component.
successCriteria: The code includes a valid import statement that imports React and useState from the 'react' package.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported React and useState. This gives you access to React's core functionality and the useState hook for managing state.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but the import statement isn't quite complete. Make sure you're importing both React and useState from 'react'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The import statement is missing or incorrect. You need to import React and useState from the 'react' package to proceed.

steps.title: Create the main App component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named App that returns null for now. This will be the main component of our application.
steps.hint: You can use either a function declaration or arrow function. Remember to import React if needed.
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState } from 'react';

// Create the App component here
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have a functional component named App that currently returns null.
successCriteria: The code must include a component named App that returns null. It can be either a function declaration or arrow function.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the App component. This gives us a foundation to build our re-render demonstration.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you've created a component named App that returns null. Check that you've used the correct syntax for a functional component.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component wasn't created correctly. You need to define a functional component named App that returns null.

steps.title: Initialize count state with useState
steps.instruction: Inside the App component, use the useState hook to create a state variable called 'count' initialized to 0. Remember to use TypeScript's generic syntax to specify the type as number.
steps.hint: Use useState<number>(0) to create a count state variable with an initial value of 0.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of initializing a numeric state variable
const [count, setCount] = useState<number>(0);
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component will have a count state variable initialized to 0, ready to be displayed and updated in later steps.
successCriteria: useState hook is called
State variable is named 'count'
Initial value is 0
TypeScript generic <number> is used
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully initialized the count state variable with useState<number>(0). This creates a reactive state that will trigger re-renders when updated.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check: Did you name the variable 'count'? Did you use useState<number>(0) with the correct initial value and TypeScript type?
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. Inside the App component, use useState<number>(0) to create a count state variable. The syntax should look like: const [count, setCount] = useState<number>(0);

steps.title: Initialize isActive state with useState
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, create a new state variable called 'isActive' using useState. Initialize it with the boolean value false. Use TypeScript generics to explicitly type it as boolean.
steps.hint: Add another useState call similar to your count state, but with a different variable name and initial value.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of adding a separate boolean state
const [isActive, setIsActive] = useState<boolean>(false);
steps.expectedOutcome: Your component will have two separate state variables: count and isActive, both managed by useState hooks.
successCriteria: Add useState hook for isActive
Variable name is 'isActive'
Initial value is false
Use TypeScript generics <boolean>
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added a second state variable. Having multiple independent states in a component is common, but can lead to unnecessary re-renders when they update separately.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check: Did you name the variable 'isActive'? Did you initialize it with 'false'? Did you include the TypeScript generic <boolean>?
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's focus on just adding the isActive state. Use the useState hook with <boolean> generic and initialize it to false.

steps.title: Define handleIncrement handler
steps.instruction: Inside your component, define a function named handleIncrement that increments the count state by 1.
steps.hint: Create a function that calls setCount with the current count plus 1.
steps.expectedOutcome: A handleIncrement function that updates the count state when called.
successCriteria: The code should include a function named handleIncrement that uses setCount to increment the count value.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the handleIncrement function that will update the count state.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your function is named handleIncrement and properly increments the count value using setCount.
steps.feedbackWrong: The handleIncrement function is missing or doesn't properly increment the count state. Try creating a function that calls setCount with the current count plus 1.

steps.title: Define handleToggle handler
steps.instruction: Define a function named handleToggle that toggles the isActive state between true and false.
steps.hint: Use the setIsActive setter function to update the state based on the previous value.
steps.expectedOutcome: A handleToggle function that toggles the isActive state when called.
successCriteria: Function named handleToggle is defined
Function uses setIsActive to toggle state
Function uses previous state (prev => !prev) or equivalent
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully defined the handleToggle function that toggles the isActive state.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure handleToggle uses setIsActive to toggle the state based on the previous value.
steps.feedbackWrong: The handleToggle function isn't quite right. It should toggle the isActive state when called.

steps.title: Return a wrapper div from App
steps.instruction: In your App component, return a single <div> element from the component.
steps.hint: The return statement should output a JSX <div> element. This will serve as the container for your UI.
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component now returns a JSX <div> element, establishing the basic structure for the UI.
successCriteria: The component returns a single JSX <div> element
The <div> is placed inside the return statement
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've added the container <div> that will hold all your UI elements.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're returning a <div> element directly from the component's return statement.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component should return a single <div> element. Check that your return statement contains a <div>.

steps.title: Add a heading to display the component name
steps.instruction: Inside the wrapper div, add an h1 element with the text 'App Component'.
steps.hint:
Add

App Component

as the first element inside the opening and closing div tags.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of adding a heading inside a div

My Component
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a visible heading 'App Component' at the top of the UI.
successCriteria: The code should contain an h1 element with the exact text 'App Component' inside the wrapper div.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've added a heading to identify the component. This static content will help demonstrate re-renders later.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added a heading, but check that it's an h1 element with the exact text 'App Component' inside the wrapper div.
steps.feedbackWrong:
The heading wasn't added correctly. Make sure to add

App Component

inside the wrapper div.

steps.title: Display the current count value
steps.instruction: Inside the wrapper div, add a paragraph element that displays the current count value. Use JSX curly braces to embed the count state variable.
steps.hint:
Add

Count: {count}

inside the existing div element.
steps.expectedOutcome: The UI will show the current count value inside a paragraph element.
successCriteria:
The code must contain a paragraph element (

) that displays the count state variable using JSX curly braces.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully displayed the current count value in the UI. This allows users to see the state value update when it changes.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're displaying the count variable inside the paragraph using JSX curly braces like {count}.
steps.feedbackWrong: The paragraph element should display the count state variable. Check that you're using the correct variable name and JSX syntax.

steps.title: Add increment button and wire onClick
steps.instruction: Add a button element inside the wrapper div with the text 'Increment' and wire its onClick event to the handleIncrement handler.
steps.hint: Use the <button> tag with onClick={handleIncrement} and the text content 'Increment'.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of adding a button with onClick handler
<button onClick={handleIncrement}>Increment</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: A button labeled 'Increment' appears in the UI, and clicking it will increase the count value.
successCriteria: Button element with text 'Increment'
onClick prop set to handleIncrement
Button placed inside the wrapper div
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added a button that triggers the count update when clicked.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you've added a button with the exact text 'Increment' and wired its onClick to handleIncrement.
steps.feedbackWrong: The button isn't properly set up. Check that you've added a <button> element with onClick={handleIncrement} and the text 'Increment' inside the wrapper div.

steps.title: Display the current isActive value
steps.instruction: Add a paragraph element inside the wrapper div that displays the current value of the isActive state.
steps.hint:
Use JSX curly braces to embed the isActive variable value inside a

tag.
steps.analogousExample:
// Displaying a boolean state value in JSX

Active status: {isActive}
steps.expectedOutcome: The UI will show the current boolean value of isActive (true or false) in a paragraph element.
successCriteria:
Add a

element
Display the isActive variable value inside the paragraph using JSX curly braces
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully displayed the isActive state value in the UI. The paragraph will show 'true' or 'false' depending on the current state.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're displaying the actual isActive variable value inside the paragraph using JSX curly braces like {isActive}.
steps.feedbackWrong:

steps.title: Add toggle button and wire onClick
steps.instruction: Add a button element with the text 'Toggle Active' inside the wrapper div, and wire its onClick event to the handleToggle handler.
steps.hint: Add a <button> element with onClick={handleToggle} and the text 'Toggle Active' between the existing elements in the wrapper div.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of adding a button with onClick wired to a handler
<button onClick={handleToggle}>Toggle Active</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a button that toggles the isActive state when clicked.
successCriteria: The button element must be present with the text 'Toggle Active' and its onClick must be set to handleToggle.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added the toggle button and wired it to the handler.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you've added a button with the exact text 'Toggle Active' and wired its onClick to handleToggle.
steps.feedbackWrong: The toggle button is missing or not correctly wired. Add a <button> element with onClick={handleToggle} and the text 'Toggle Active'.
